subtype: Approach: task decomposition with a shared board [Action]
passage: Saurabh, you asked how our final-year team didn't fall apart. I'm Raghav, so you'll get the honest version. Four of us, one crop-disease detection app, eight months. In the first week we broke the project into modules: image collection, the model, the app screens, and the report. Then we broke each module into tasks small enough to finish in under a week and put them on a shared online board. Every task had one owner's name and a date. Not "the team". One name. Every Monday and Thursday at 5, we met for fifteen minutes, standing, in the lab corridor. Each person said what they'd finished, what was next, and what was blocking them. That's it. When Pooja's image collection slipped by a week, we saw it on a Thursday, not in March. Honestly, the board did half the managing for us.

qa.q: When did the team meet each week?
qa.a: Every Monday and Thursday at 5, for fifteen minutes.

qa.q: How does Raghav feel about the board?
qa.a: Raghav sounds proud and relieved, crediting the board with doing half the managing.

qa.q: What else could Saurabh's team add to this system?
qa.a: They could list risks on the board too, so problems like slipping data collection are flagged before they happen.

qa.q: How was Pooja affected by the twice-weekly reviews?
qa.a: Pooja's delay was spotted early, so the team could help while there was still time, rather than it becoming a crisis later.

grounding: Shows a team of four splitting the project into modules, putting tasks with owners and dates on a shared board, and reviewing it briefly twice a week.

subtype: Approach: task decomposition with a shared board [Action]
passage: Our team sat at the next table in the project lab, so I watched Jatin and Kavitha's group get organised while we argued. On day one, Kavitha drew four columns on the whiteboard: To do, Doing, Review, Done. Jatin broke their traffic-signal project into modules: camera input, vehicle counting, signal logic, dashboard. Each module was split into small tasks on sticky notes, each with one name and a date. Later they moved it all to an online board. Every Tuesday and Friday, the four of them stood around a laptop for ten minutes and went through it. Once I heard Jatin say, "The counting is stuck because I'm waiting for Kavitha's camera code." Kavitha moved her card to the top. I don't know whether they ever fought in private. But by December their board was mostly in Done, and ours was still an argument.

qa.q: What columns did Kavitha draw?
qa.a: To do, Doing, Review, Done.

qa.q: What might Jatin have felt when the counting was stuck?
qa.a: Jatin was likely frustrated at waiting but said so calmly, and probably felt relieved when Kavitha moved her card to the top.

qa.q: What else could the observer's team borrow from this?
qa.a: They could split their project into small tasks with one owner and a date each, and hold a short review twice a week.

qa.q: How does the observer see their own team compared with Jatin's?
qa.a: The observer sees Jatin's team moving steadily while their own team is still arguing, and seems a little envious.

grounding: Illustrates a team of four breaking a project into modules on a shared board with owners and dates and reviewing it twice a week.

subtype: Approach: dependency and critical-path thinking [Thinking]
passage:
Subject: Changing our plan this week (please read before Friday)
Hi all,
I spent last night drawing our project as boxes and arrows, and I think we've been working in the wrong order.
Model training (Aman's part) can't start until the data pipeline (Binita's part) is working. No clean data, no model. The interface (mine and Ritika's) doesn't depend on either. We can build it with sample data now and plug the real model in later.
So the pipeline is the thing everything waits on. Right now Binita is doing it alone while three of us polish screens.
Proposal: for the next two weeks, Aman helps Binita with the pipeline, since he needs its output anyway. Ritika and I carry on with the interface in parallel. Once the pipeline runs, Aman switches to training.
Binita, does this help, or would you rather split it differently?
Dhruv

qa.q: Whose part is the data pipeline?
qa.a: Binita's part.

qa.q: What was Dhruv worried about?
qa.a: Dhruv was worried the team had been working in the wrong order, leaving Binita alone on the part everything waits on.

qa.q: What else could help the pipeline move faster?
qa.a: The team could agree a simple sample data format early, so Aman can start testing small model pieces while the full pipeline is finished.

qa.q: How might Binita see the proposal?
qa.a: Binita, who has been doing the pipeline alone, would likely feel relieved and supported, and is invited to shape the split.

grounding: Shows a team member seeing that the data pipeline must come before model training while the interface can run in parallel, so the pipeline owner gets help first.

subtype: Approach: dependency and critical-path thinking [Thinking]
passage: Anjali, you asked why our team started helping Sohail in week five. I'm Irawati. Our project was a model that predicts crop prices, with a web interface. Four parts: data pipeline, model, interface, report. For a month, everyone worked on their own part. Then one night I drew it as a chain. The model needs cleaned data. The data needs Sohail's pipeline. So if Sohail is late, the model is late, and so is everything after it. But the interface? It only needs a sample output file. We could build it any time. That's when I saw that the pipeline was the one link nothing could skip. Everything else could wait; that couldn't. So I moved from the report, which had loads of slack, to help Sohail with data cleaning. Two weeks later the pipeline ran, and the model team finally had something real to train on.

qa.q: What does the interface need?
qa.a: It only needs a sample output file.

qa.q: How did Irawati feel on drawing the chain?
qa.a: Irawati felt a flash of clarity, and some alarm, seeing that the whole project depended on Sohail's pipeline.

qa.q: What else could the team do once the pipeline runs?
qa.a: They could redraw the chain to find the next step everything depends on, such as model training, and move help there.

qa.q: How might Sohail have experienced the extra help?
qa.a: Sohail, likely under pressure as the part everyone waited on, probably felt relieved when Irawati joined.

grounding: Illustrates a student mapping which parts depend on which, seeing the data pipeline must come before training, and moving help to the pipeline.

subtype: Approach: minimum viable version first [Action]
passage:
Dear Ganga Chechi,
Last year you told me, "Get something working first, then make it clever." I thought you were being boring. You were right.
Our final-year project is an attendance system for the college. The plan had face recognition, automatic reports, a parent app, everything. But after your advice, we built the plainest possible version first: teachers tap names on a tablet, it saves them, and it shows who is absent. It took us three weeks.
Then we added face recognition, which took two months and broke three times. Then reports.
Last week our guide moved our demo two weeks earlier. Other teams panicked. We didn't, because the basic version had worked since August. We showed that, plus face recognition in one classroom.
Thank you, Chechi. Next time I'll call it wise, not boring.
Love,
Elizabeth

qa.q: How long did the plain version take?
qa.a: It took us three weeks.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel when the demo was moved earlier?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt calm and a little proud while other teams panicked, since the basic version had worked since August.

qa.q: What else could the team do before the final demo?
qa.a: They could test face recognition in more classrooms and keep the basic tap-names version ready as a backup.

qa.q: How might Ganga Chechi feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Ganga Chechi would likely feel pleased and amused that the boring advice turned out to be wise.

grounding: Shows a team building a bare working attendance system in three weeks before adding face recognition and reports, so a demo exists when time runs short.

subtype: Approach: minimum viable version first [Action]
passage: Our final-year project? Okay. I'm Kalyani, and I'll tell you the part nobody puts in the report. Asif, my teammate, wanted to start with face recognition, because that's the exciting bit. I said, first let's build something ugly that works. So in three weeks we made a web page where the teacher types the roll numbers of students present, it saves them, and it shows who's absent. No faces. Asif called it "a glorified register." Then we started the face part. It was brilliant in the lab and terrible under classroom tube lights. Two weeks before the external demo, the camera module stopped working completely. Asif looked sick. I said, "We still have the glorified register." We demoed that, showed face recognition as a recorded video, and passed comfortably. Asif bought me cutting chai for a week.

qa.q: What did Asif call the plain version?
qa.a: A glorified register.

qa.q: How did Asif feel when the camera module failed?
qa.a: Asif was dismayed and anxious, looking sick two weeks before the demo.

qa.q: What else could the team have done with the face part?

qa.q: How might the external examiner see the demo?
qa.a: The examiner sees a working system plus a video of the face feature, which is enough to pass comfortably even though the camera failed.

grounding: Illustrates a team building a plain working attendance version first and adding face recognition later, so a demo still exists when the camera fails.

subtype: Approach: leaving work to the last month [Pitfall]
passage: I live two doors down from Pranav in the hostel, so I saw his project year from the corridor. In August, he and Alka told everyone their inventory app was easy. "Two weeks of coding, max." September and October were cricket and fest season. In November they said, "After the mid-terms." In the first week of March, a month before submission, I started hearing keyboards at 2 am. Alka came over most nights with her laptop. The login module worked on Pranav's machine and crashed on hers. The database didn't talk to the app. One night I heard Pranav say, "Nothing fits together." They submitted on the last day, with a video instead of a live demo, because the live version kept freezing. I don't know how they felt about it. They didn't talk about the project for weeks after.

qa.q: When did the late-night coding begin?
qa.a: In the first week of March, a month before submission.

qa.q: What might Pranav have been feeling when he said nothing fits together?
qa.a: Pranav was probably panicked and exhausted, realising the parts they had assumed were easy would not join up.

qa.q: What else could the pair have done in August?
qa.a: They could have built a small working version early and joined the parts from the start, so joining problems showed up in time.

qa.q: How is Alka affected by the late start?
qa.a: Alka ends up coding most nights and dealing with crashes on her own laptop, sharing the stress of the rushed finish.

grounding: Shows a team sure the project is easy putting off coding until the last month, then hitting integration bugs and submitting a barely working version.

subtype: Approach: leaving work to the last month [Pitfall]
passage:
August. Kunal and Sunaina read their project brief, a campus lost-and-found app, and laughed. "We can build this in two weekends." They told their guide they'd start after the fest.
March. With four weeks left, they finally opened the code editor. The upload page worked alone. The search page worked alone. Together, they crashed. Sunaina's database design didn't match what Kunal's screens expected. They stayed in the lab until the guard switched off the lights, three nights in a row. Kunal's eyes were red; Sunaina stopped answering her family's calls.
April. On submission day, their app ran only if nobody searched with a space in the words. In the viva, the external examiner typed "blue bottle". The screen froze. Kunal stared at the floor. Sunaina said quietly, "We started too late, sir." The examiner nodded and wrote something down.

qa.q: What was the project?
qa.a: A campus lost-and-found app.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when the screen froze?
qa.a: Kunal felt ashamed and defeated, staring at the floor.

qa.q: What would you change first about their plan?
qa.a: Start in August with a small version that connects the upload and search pages early, so mismatches show up months before the viva.

qa.q: How might the external examiner see the project?
qa.a: The examiner sees a fragile app and an honest admission, likely judging that the idea was fine but the planning was not.

grounding: Illustrates a team that thought the project easy leaving coding to the final month, then facing integration bugs and a barely working submission.

subtype: Approach: groupthink on the first idea [Pitfall]
passage:
"So, status update. Aditya, you had the dataset?"
"Working on it."
"It's week seven."
"Look, Suraj, a dataset of street-food hygiene photos from Indian cities is out there somewhere. I've emailed three labs."
"Any replies?"
"...Not yet."
Hafsa put her pen down. "Can I say something? I wasn't sure this dataset existed even in week one."
"Then why didn't you say?"
"Because you were so sure, Aditya, and everyone clapped. It felt rude."
Suraj rubbed his face. "I had the same doubt. I searched for two nights in week two and found nothing. I thought I was just bad at searching."
"So two of you knew?"
"Suspected. We should have said it out loud."
"Okay. Seven weeks gone. What now?"
"Now we talk to the guide tomorrow, and look for a topic with data we can actually see."

qa.q: What week is it at the status update?
qa.a: It's week seven.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa stay quiet at the start?
qa.a: Hafsa felt it would be rude to question Aditya, who seemed so sure and everyone clapped, so the doubt was swallowed.

qa.q: What else could the team have done in week one?
qa.a: They could have asked each member to write doubts privately before agreeing, and checked that a dataset existed before committing.

qa.q: How might Aditya feel hearing that two teammates doubted it all along?
qa.a: Aditya may feel embarrassed and a bit hurt that nobody spoke up earlier, when changing course would have been easy.

grounding: Shows a team going along with the loudest member's topic while two members privately doubt the dataset exists, a doubt that surfaces only after weeks.

subtype: Approach: groupthink on the first idea [Pitfall]
passage: In our final year, Karan suggested a project predicting bus arrival times in our city from live GPS data. He was so excited that we all said yes in the first meeting. I'm Seema. That night I tried to find the live bus data. I couldn't. I told myself it probably needed special access and Karan must know how. My friend Sarika, it turned out, had the same doubt; she had searched for an hour and found only old timetables. Neither of us said anything. It felt disloyal to question the idea everyone loved. For six weeks we built screens and wrote the literature review. Then our guide asked, "Where is your data from?" Karan went pale. There was no live feed we could use. We had to change the topic in week seven and redo half the work. Looking back, two quiet doubts in week one could have saved six weeks.

qa.q: What did Sarika find?
qa.a: Only old timetables.

qa.q: Why did Seema keep quiet about the doubt?
qa.a: Seema felt it would be disloyal to question the idea everyone loved, and hoped Karan must know how to get the data.

qa.q: What else could the team have done in the first meeting?
qa.a: They could have made checking the data source the first task before saying yes, and invited everyone to voice doubts openly.

qa.q: How might Karan have felt when the guide asked about data?
qa.a: Karan went pale, likely shocked and embarrassed that his exciting idea had no usable data behind it.

grounding: Illustrates a team accepting the most enthusiastic member's topic while two members quietly doubt the data exists, until the problem surfaces weeks later.

subtype: Approach: divergent brainstorming then voting [Thinking]
passage: In the engineering college outside Hassan, the project room had a slow ceiling fan and one working plug point. Harish, usually the loudest in any group, surprised everyone. "This time, no talking for ten minutes. Everyone writes ideas alone. At least two each." Rekha, who hardly spoke in meetings, wrote four. When they pinned all ten on the soft board, hers included a moisture monitor for coffee drying yards near her village and an app to track milk collection at the local dairy. Then they scored each idea from one to five on three things: can we build it, do we care about it, and will Professor Gowda approve. The milk-collection idea came first, with top scores in the first two columns. Rekha went red. "I didn't think anyone would pick mine." Harish grinned. "Nobody picked it. The numbers did."

qa.q: How many ideas did Rekha write?
qa.a: Rekha wrote four.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel when her idea came first?
qa.a: Rekha felt shy and surprised, going red because she never expected her idea to be chosen.

qa.q: What else could keep quieter members heard later in the project?
qa.a: The team could keep writing silently before discussing at key decisions, like choosing features, not only at the start.

qa.q: How does Harish see the silent writing?
qa.a: Harish, usually the loudest, sees it as a way to let everyone contribute, and credits the scores rather than taking the credit.

subtype: Approach: divergent brainstorming then voting [Thinking]
passage: In a borrowed tutorial room at the university in Lagos, Chidi handed out sticky notes. "Five minutes. Write project ideas. Don't show anyone yet." Sami, who had barely spoken in their first two meetings, filled three notes before anyone else finished one. When the ten notes went up on the wall, one of Sami's read: "Offline app for market traders to track stock without data." Ada had written "drone delivery", which she admitted was mostly for fun. They scored every idea from one to five on how buildable it was, how much they cared, and whether their supervisor would approve. Drone delivery got a five for interest and a one for buildability. Sami's market app got fours across the board and came out on top. Sami smiled at the table, then looked up. "I nearly didn't write that one," Sami said. "It felt too small."

qa.a: Ada seems relaxed about it, having written it mostly for fun, and the scores made the loss feel fair.

subtype: Approach: one member does everything [Pitfall]
passage: By October, Yusuf had quietly rewritten most of the team's hospital-queue app. "It's faster if I just do it," he'd say, and push new code at 2 am. Ira and the other two stopped opening the project. Why fix what Yusuf would redo by morning? Then came the complication: the viva, planned for late April, was pulled forward to the first week of April because the external examiner had to travel. There was no time left to catch up. On the day, the examiner pointed at Ira. "Explain how your app decides the queue order." Ira looked at the screen. She had written the first version of that logic in August. None of it was left. "I think... Yusuf changed it." The examiner turned to the other two, who also looked at Yusuf. Yusuf explained it perfectly. The examiner wrote: "Only one member understands the project."

qa.q: When was the viva moved to?
qa.a: To the first week of April.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when asked to explain?
qa.a: Ira felt lost and embarrassed, since the logic she once wrote had been completely replaced.

qa.q: What would you change first in how Yusuf worked?
qa.a: Yusuf could explain each change in short team sessions or pair with a teammate on each module, so everyone keeps ownership and understanding.

qa.q: How might Yusuf feel reading the examiner's note?
qa.a: Yusuf may feel uneasy that taking over, meant to help, left the whole team marked down.

grounding: Shows the strongest coder taking over instead of explaining, so teammates lose ownership and cannot explain their own project at an earlier-than-planned viva.

subtype: Approach: one member does everything [Pitfall]
passage: In a Chennai college's project lab, Pankaj had the fastest fingers anyone had seen. When Chandrika's database design had a flaw in September, he fixed it overnight, and redesigned it while he was at it. When the map screen lagged, he rewrote it. By December the team's e-waste pickup app was ninety percent his code. Chandrika kept writing the report, describing features she hadn't touched. She told herself it was fine; the app worked, and it looked beautiful. At the viva in April, the examiner asked her, "Why did you choose this table structure?" Chandrika opened her mouth. It was no longer her structure. "Pankaj changed it," she said, and felt her face burn. The examiner asked the third member about the map. Same answer. Pankaj, sitting at the end, looked at his hands. Their marks came back uneven, and the report was flagged for review.

qa.q: How much of the app was Pankaj's code by December?
qa.a: Ninety percent.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel at the viva?
qa.a: Chandrika felt ashamed, her face burning, unable to explain a structure that was no longer hers.

qa.q: What else could the team have done in September?
qa.a: They could have agreed that Pankaj reviews and explains fixes instead of rewriting, so Chandrika keeps ownership of the database.

qa.q: How might Pankaj feel at the end of the viva?
qa.a: Pankaj seems uneasy, looking at his hands, perhaps realising that doing everything left his teammates unable to speak for their own project.

grounding: Illustrates the strongest coder rewriting teammates' parts instead of explaining, so at the viva the others cannot explain the project.

subtype: Approach: negotiating roles by strength and interest [Action]
passage:
"Before we split anything, everyone says two things. What you're good at, and what you want to learn this year. Gautam, you start."
"Good at: backend, databases. Want to learn: front end. I've never done any, and that scares me a bit."
"Tenzin?"

"So everyone has something to show at the viva."
"Exactly. Nobody is just the slides person."

subtype: Approach: negotiating roles by strength and interest [Action]
passage: Our final-year team almost split up in the first month. I'm Chaitanya. Vishal and I both wanted the machine learning part, because it looked best on a resume, and nobody wanted the documentation. So our guide made the four of us sit in the library for an hour and say two things each: what we're good at, and what we want to learn. It felt awkward. But Vishal admitted he'd already done machine learning in an internship and actually wanted to learn app development. I admitted I was strong in data cleaning but had never trained a model. Neha, the quiet one, said she loved writing and wanted to try testing. Suddenly it fit. I took the model, Vishal took the app, Neha took documentation plus testing, and Arif took the data pipeline. Each of us also reviewed one other part every week. At the viva, all four of us could answer questions.

qa.q: How did Vishal benefit from the candid meeting?
qa.a: Vishal got to learn app development, which he actually wanted, instead of repeating machine learning just for the resume.

subtype: Approach: buffer planning before the viva [Action]
passage: I'm the lab assistant in the computer science block, so I see every final-year team in the last month. Most of them are here at midnight in April. Hemant and Pranav's team was different. In January, Hemant wrote on the lab whiteboard: "Code freeze: 15 March. Deadline: 31 March." Pranav asked why so early. Hemant said, "Because something will go wrong, and I don't know what yet." They froze their code on the 15th. On the 18th, testing found a bug in the payment screen that took four days to fix. On the 24th, the report printer broke and they had to reprint elsewhere. On the 28th, they rehearsed the viva twice in this room. On the 31st, they submitted at eleven in the morning and went for lunch. I can't read minds, but they didn't look like people who'd been up all night.

qa.q: What was the code freeze date?
qa.a: 15 March.

qa.q: Why did Hemant want the code freeze so early?
qa.a: Hemant felt sure something would go wrong and was wary of surprises, wanting time left to handle them.

qa.q: What else could the team add to the final fortnight?
qa.a: They could ask someone outside the team to try the app, since fresh eyes often find bugs the builders miss.

qa.q: How does the lab assistant see this team compared with others?
qa.a: The lab assistant notices they finish calmly and go for lunch, while most teams are in the lab at midnight in April.

grounding: Shows a team finishing coding two weeks early and keeping the last fortnight for testing, the report and rehearsal, expecting something to slip.

subtype: Approach: buffer planning before the viva [Action]
passage:
January. Aparna set out the project calendar in the team's shared sheet. "Coding ends on 1 March. The deadline is 15 March. Those two weeks are for testing, printing the report and one full rehearsal." Chetan frowned. "That's two weeks of not coding." "That's two weeks of fixing whatever breaks," Aparna said.
1 March. They stopped adding features, though Chetan had one more idea he loved. Aparna wrote it on a list titled "After the viva".
9 March. Testing had found three bugs; two were fixed in a day, one took four. The report was printed. On the 13th they rehearsed the viva in front of two juniors, who asked about data privacy, a question none of them had prepared for. They worked out an answer together that evening. On the 15th, when the examiner asked the very same privacy question, Chetan answered it smoothly and glanced at Aparna.

qa.q: When did coding end?
qa.a: Coding ends on 1 March.

qa.q: How did Chetan feel about stopping coding on 1 March?
qa.a: Chetan was reluctant, having one more idea he loved, and frowned at two weeks without coding.

qa.q: What else could the team do with ideas like Chetan's?
qa.a: Keep them on the After the viva list and choose the best for a later version, so ideas aren't lost but don't threaten the deadline.

qa.q: How might the two juniors see the rehearsal?
qa.a: The juniors get a preview of a viva and help the team by asking a question they hadn't prepared for.

grounding: Illustrates a team planning to stop coding two weeks before the deadline, using the buffer for testing, the report and a rehearsal that pays off.

subtype: Approach: root-cause analysis of a missed milestone [Revision]
passage: The second missed milestone hit Arohi's team on a Sunday, in a café near their Bengaluru college. The login and profile module was supposed to be done. Again, it wasn't. Tanvir, who owned it, looked ready to be blamed. Arohi took a napkin. "Let's just ask why. Five times, if we need to." Why isn't it done? Because Tanvir kept rewriting it. Why? Because each time he showed it, someone wanted something different. Why? Because nobody had ever written down what the profile page should include. Why not? Because they'd agreed it on a voice call and everyone remembered it differently. Tanvir let out a long breath. "So I'm not slow. I was chasing a moving target." That evening they wrote a one-page spec for every module, with one line at the top: "Done means it works, it's tested, and all four of us have seen it."

qa.q: Where did the team meet on Sunday?
qa.a: In a café near their Bengaluru college.

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel after the whys?
qa.a: Tanvir felt relieved, letting out a long breath on seeing the delay was not laziness but a moving target.

qa.q: What else could the team do when a new idea comes up mid-module?
qa.a: They could add it to the spec only after everyone agrees and adjust the date, so the target doesn't move quietly.

qa.q: How might Arohi see the root cause?
qa.a: Arohi sees it as a team gap in writing things down, not one person's fault, which is why the fix is a spec for every module.

grounding: Shows a team asking why repeatedly after a milestone slips twice, finding unclear requirements rather than laziness, and writing a spec and definition of done.

subtype: Approach: root-cause analysis of a missed milestone [Revision]
passage:
"That's the second time the dashboard milestone slipped, Nikita."
"I know, Lavanya. I'm sorry."
"I'm not asking for sorry. I'm asking why. Why isn't it done?"
"Because I had to redo the charts."
"Why?"
"Because on Tuesday Rohan said he wanted weekly data, and on Thursday you said monthly."
"...Did I?"
"You did. Why did we say different things?"
"Because we never wrote down what the dashboard is for."
"Why not?"
"Because we thought it was obvious."
"So it's not that you're slow."
"No. It's that nobody knew what finished looked like."
"Okay. Tonight we write one page. Who uses the dashboard, what it shows, weekly or monthly. And a definition of done: it works, it's tested, and all four of us have signed off."
"Can we add: nobody changes it without telling everyone?"
"Yes. That too."

qa.a: Rohan wanted weekly data.

qa.q: What else could the team do to stop this in other modules?
qa.a: They could write a one-page spec for each module before starting, saying who uses it and what done means.

qa.q: How does Lavanya see the missed milestone by the end?
qa.a: Lavanya realises that a changing request from Lavanya was part of the cause, seeing unclear requirements rather than slowness.
